metadata.title: Shannon Shakes Hands with Chernoff: Big Data Viewpoint On Channel Information Measures

nodes.name: Chernoff Mutual Information Formula
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} I_C(X,Y) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {\sum\limits_y {{p^\alpha }(x,y){{(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }}} } } \right). \end{aligned}

nodes.name: BSC Shannon Mutual Information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^2 {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^2 {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr & = (1 - \varepsilon )\log {{1 - \varepsilon } \over {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon }} + \varepsilon \log {\varepsilon \over {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )}}. \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.label: BSC Mutual information

nodes.name: BSC Chernoff Mutual Information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ &=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log ( {(1 - \varepsilon )^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon } \right)^{1 - \alpha }} \\ &+ {\varepsilon ^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )} \right)^{1 - \alpha }} ) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: BSC Chernoff information

nodes.name: MSC Shannon Mutual Information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^M {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^M {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.label: MSC Mutual information

nodes.name: MSC Chernoff Mutual Information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {{p(xy)}^\alpha (x){(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ \end{aligned}
nodes.label: MSC Chernoff information

nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} Y = f\left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \overset{(a)}{=}{\theta ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right)= \psi \left( {\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} \right)\\ \end{aligned}

nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \varPsi=\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \end{aligned}

nodes.name: ACE Algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{ACE Algorithm} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;\\ \STATE End Inner Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;\\ \STATE End Outer Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;\\ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Alternately regresses theta(Y) against the current sum of phi_i(X_i) until the normalized residual stops decreasing.
nodes.label: alg:ACE

nodes.name: Simulation Procedure
nodes.statement: \caption*{Simulation Procedure} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$; \STATE Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information; \STATE Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm; \STATE Repeat above process till the required times. \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Generate random channel parameters, compute Shannon/Chernoff mutual information, decompose by ACE, and repeat.
nodes.label: alg:simulated

nodes.name: Shannon Mutual Information
nodes.statement: The mutual information is a measure of the amount of information that one random variable contains about another variable. In fact, it describes the reduction in the uncertainty of one random variable if another one is known [\cite{Elements}]. According to [\cite{Elements}], the Shannon mutual information is defined as: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & I_S(X,Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{x,y} {p(x,y)log{{p(x,y)} \over {p(x)p(y)}}} \cr \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $X,Y$ are two random variables with marginal probability mass functions $p(x)$ and $p(y)$ and joint probability mass function $p(x,y)$. It is noted that $I(X;Y)$ is the relative entropy (or Kullback-leibler distance) between the joint distribution $p(x,y)$ and the product distribution $p(x)p(y)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2006
differentia: between the joint distribution $p(x,y)$ and the product distribution $p(x)p(y)$
nodes.statement_short: KL divergence $D(p(x,y)\|p(x)p(y))$ between the joint and product distributions of $X,Y$.

nodes.name: Relative Entropy (Kullback-Leibler Distance)
nodes.statement: The relative entropy is given by [\cite{Elements}]: \begin{equation} D(p||q) = \sum\limits_{x \in \textit{X}} {p(x)log{{p(x)} \over {q(x)}}} \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2006

nodes.name: Chernoff Information
nodes.statement: The Chernoff information is derived from the problem of classic hypothesis testing. Chernoff Information is the resulting error exponent when minimizing the overall probability of error [\cite{Elements}]. As defined in [\cite{Elements}], it is given by \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} I_C({{\rm{P}}_1},{P_2}) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\alpha$ is real parameter with $0\leq \alpha \leq 1$.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2006
differentia: when minimizing the overall probability of error
nodes.statement_short: Error exponent minimizing the worst-case probability of error between two distributions $P_1,P_2$ (Chernoff bound).

nodes.name: Chernoff Mutual Information
nodes.statement: With the aid of Chernoff information to describe the relationship between the two variables, a new mutual information is defined as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} I_C(X,Y) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {\sum\limits_y {{p^\alpha }(x,y){{(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }}} } } \right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} In this paper, we call it Chernoff mutual information relative to Shannon mutual information.
nodes.statement_short: This paper's two-variable analogue of Chernoff information, used as an alternative channel mutual-information measure.

nodes.name: Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC)
nodes.statement: Consider the BSC, which is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelBSC}. It is a binary channel where the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$. The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $. It is argued in [\cite{Elements}] that it reflects common characteristics of the general channel with errors though it is the simplest model.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2006
differentia: the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$
The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $
nodes.statement_short: A binary channel with input probabilities $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$ and symmetric transmission error $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Multiple Symmetric Channel (MSC)
nodes.statement: The MSC is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelMBSC}. The number of input symbol is $M$. The probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$).The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$. The BSC is the special case of MSC for $M=2$.
differentia: the number of input symbol is $M$
the probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$)
The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$
nodes.statement_short: An $M$-ary symmetric channel generalizing BSC, with input probabilities $(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_M)$ and per-symbol error $\varepsilon/(M-1)$.

nodes.name: ACE Algorithm (Alternating Conditional Expectation)
nodes.statement: Much of research in regression analysis has examined the optimal transformation between one or more predictors and the response. Unlike traditional multiple regression algorithm which requires the priori information of the functional forms, the ACE algorithm of Breiman and Friedman (1985) in [\cite{breiman1985estimating}] does not require that and it is non-parametric transformation. That is to say, it is a fully automated algorithm to estimate the optimal transformation between predictors and response. Furthermore, it can be also used to estimate maximal correlation among random variables. The implementation of the ACE algorithm can consult [\cite{breiman1985estimating}][\cite{wang2004estimating}].
differentia: estimate the optimal transformation between predictors and response
can be also used to estimate maximal correlation among random variables
nodes.statement_short: Non-parametric Breiman-Friedman algorithm that estimates optimal variable transformations and maximal correlation.

nodes.name: ACE Residual Error
nodes.statement: Assume random variables $X_1,X_2,\cdots ,X_p$ are predictors and $Y$ is response. Supposing $\phi _1(X_1),\phi _2(X_2),\cdots,\phi _p(X_p),\theta (Y)$ are arbitrary zero mean functions of the corresponding variables, the residual error is \begin{equation} {e^2}\left( {\theta ,{\phi _1},\cdots,{\phi _p}} \right) = {{E\left\{ {{{\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right]}^2}} \right\}} \over {E\left[ {{\theta ^2}(Y)} \right]}} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Normalized mean-squared residual between $\theta(Y)$ and $\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)$, minimized by the ACE iteration.

nodes.name: ACE Application to Channel Parameters
nodes.statement: In this paper, we use the ACE algorithm help us separate multivariate function. Let $X_1,X_2,\cdots,X_p$ be the channel parameters and $Y$ be measured value of channel information. The functional relation between them is: \begin{equation} Y = f({X_1},{X_2},...,{X_p}). \end{equation} It is supposed that ${X_1},{X_2},...,{X_p}$ are known and independent. Moreover, the functional relation $f$ is also known since it is defined by human to describe the channel information. Therefore, it is easy to get $Y$ and they form a data set $\{Y,X_1,\cdots,X_p\}$. This data set meets the precondition of the ACE algorithm, so ACE algorithm can be used to analyze them. As a result, one can get \begin{equation} \theta (Y) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}(X_i)} + \delta \end{equation} where $\delta$ is residual error. In this case, it is easy to find out the separate influence of each correspondent channel parameter.
nodes.statement_short: Applies ACE to decompose a channel-information measure $Y=f(\mathbf{X})$ into per-parameter functions $\phi_i(X_i)$ plus residual $\delta$.

nodes.name: Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Model
nodes.statement: In fact, the probably approximately correct (PAC) model is enough for us in most of time [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}]. In this model, one only need to construct algorithms which guarantee that it is correct with high probability (not necessarily one). This model is the foundation of Support Vector Machine (SVM) [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}].
nodes.statement_short: Vapnik's PAC framework: an algorithm need only be correct with high probability, not certainty -- the basis of SVM.

nodes.name: ACE Results Function
nodes.statement: The ACE results is \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} Y = f\left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \overset{(a)}{=}{\theta ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right)= \psi \left( {\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} \right)\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $Y$ is the channel information and ${\textbf{X}}$ is all the set of all the input channel parameters. The equation ($a$) holds because the residual error $\delta$ can be ignored. From the figures above, it is noted that $ \phi_i(X_i)$ is almost the same for both Shannon and Chernoff mutual information. For these two measures, the only difference is $\theta(\cdot)$. The function $\psi(\cdot)$ is different and ${\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} $ is the same. From the Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I} to Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I}, it is also noted that the function $\theta(\cdot)$ is monotonic function.
nodes.statement_short: Writes the ACE output as $Y=\theta^{-1}(\sum\phi_i(X_i))=\psi(\varphi(\mathbf{X}))$, separating a parameter-only part $\varphi$ from a measure-specific part $\psi$.

nodes.name: Nature of Channel Information
nodes.statement: It is noted that $\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}}\right)$ in Eq.(\ref{Res_Fun}) is the same whatever we adopt the Shannon channel information measures or Chernoff channel information measures. In this paper, we take $\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}}\right)$ as the nature of channel information and we get \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \varPsi=\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the $\varPsi$ is the nature of channel information. It is only decided by the channel parameters and it contains the core of the channel information. The other physical quantity about channel information is just the function of $\varPsi$, just as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \rm{I}= \psi (\varPsi) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\rm{I}$ is a measurement of channel information. As far as Shannon mutual information and Chernoff mutual information are concerned, their only difference is the function $\psi(\cdot)$. They can be seen as a compound function. The inner is $\varPsi$ which is the function w.r.t. channel parameters and the outer is the function w.r.t. $\varPsi$. For different channel information measures, the inner is always the same but the outer is different.
nodes.statement_short: Defines $\Psi=\varphi(\mathbf{X})$, the parameter-only 'core' shared by every channel-information measure $I=\psi(\Psi)$.

nodes.name: Big Data Rules
nodes.statement: Two data rules are believed. For one thing, the data does not lie. For other thing, we only need to guarantee that our conclusion is correct with very large probability rather than one in the era of big data [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}].

nodes.name: Shannon vs. Chernoff: Different Distance Measures
nodes.statement: In fact, both Shannon mutual information and Chernoff mutual information are to depict the inner relationship between two random variables. The difference is that they adopt different measures of the distance between two distributions. The relative entropy is adopted in Shannon mutual information and the R{\'{e}}nyi divergence is used in Chernoff mutual information [\cite{van2014renyi}].

nodes.name: ACE Decomposition Validity (BSC)
nodes.statement: The correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda)+\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is extremely close to $1$. Furthermore, The error of the ACE decomposition $\delta$ is invariably near to zero. Clearly, both of them have shown that the ACE decomposition results are excellent.
conclusions: The correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda)+\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is extremely close to $1$
The error of the ACE decomposition $\delta$ is invariably near to zero

nodes.name: ACE Decomposition Validity (MSC)
nodes.statement: Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I} shows similar characteristics that in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I}. The value of the ACE decomposition error $\delta$ is still very small. On the other hand, the correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda_1)+\phi_2(\lambda_2)+\phi_3(\lambda_3)+\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is close to $1$. These two points verify the validity of the ACE algorithm again.
conclusions: the correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda_1)+\phi_2(\lambda_2)+\phi_3(\lambda_3)+\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is close to $1$
The value of the ACE decomposition error $\delta$ is still very small

nodes.name: Shannon Shakes Hands with Chernoff
nodes.statement: In this sense, Shannon shakes hands with Chernoff. Over the last decades, Shannon information and Chernoff information are always considered to be two kinds of channel information measures and the relation between them is that Kullback-Leibler divergence is the special case of R{\'{e}}nyi divergence when $\alpha=1$. The channel information measures deduced from them look very different even for the channel as simple as BSC. However, with the aid of the ACE algorithm, we find the inner relations between them. In fact, they are different metrics of the same physical quantity. For a channel, in a certain time, if all of its parameters are given, all of its state and properties will be determined. Thus the information about the same channel is always consistent. For example, the kilometer and centimeter are both measures of length, but they are used in different situations for convenience. Generally speaking, we do not adopt the centimeter to measure the distance between two cities. In contrast, we would like adopt it to measure the length of the steel rule. Their true values are identical when measuring the same things, even their numerical values are different. Similarly, the Shannon and Chernoff information are two metrics of the same quantity of information.
nodes.statement_short: Shannon and Chernoff mutual information are different metrics of the same underlying channel-information quantity (like km vs. cm for length).

nodes.name: Shannon's theta^-1 Exceeds Chernoff's
nodes.statement: As mentioned above, the curves of $\theta(\cdot)$ have the same trend and the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information. Therefore, the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's. Actually, the facts extremely agree with the this corollary, which can well explain the phenomena in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC1 C and I}.
assumptions: the curves of $\theta(\cdot)$ have the same trend
the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information
conclusions: the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's
nodes.statement_short: Since Shannon's $\theta(Y)$ is uniformly smaller and $\theta$ is monotonic, Shannon's inverse $\theta^{-1}$ exceeds Chernoff's.

nodes.name: Universal ACE-Decomposition Conjecture
nodes.statement: There is a conjecture that if a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information, it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent. This rule can be used to judge the rationality of the new information measure. This conjecture also provides a way for us to propose a new information measure for the fact that we can construct that based on designing the function $\psi(\cdot)$. In fact, even if this guess is not right with probability one, the new one which conforms to the law is correct with large probability and we can easily find the relation between that and previous information measures, such as Shannon and Chernoff information.
assumptions: a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information
conclusions: it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent
nodes.statement_short: Conjectures that any new channel-information measure will decompose via ACE into a function $\psi(\cdot)$ of the same channel 'nature' $\Psi$.

nodes.name: Simulated BSC Dataset
nodes.statement: $20000$ observations geneated from the Eq.(\ref{BSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ are independently drawn from a uniform distribution $U(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with two input parameters.

nodes.name: Simulated MSC Dataset
nodes.statement: $60000$ observations generated from the Eq.(\ref{MSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{MSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. They are generated randomly and independently, which is bound in $(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with four input parameters.

nodes.name: Initialize theta and phi
nodes.statement: set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;\\
nodes.statement_short: Initialize $\theta(Y)$ and all $\phi_i(X_i)$ to zero.

nodes.name: Outer iteration loop
nodes.statement: Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\
nodes.statement_short: Outer loop: repeat until the residual error stops decreasing.

nodes.name: Inner iteration loop
nodes.statement: Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\
nodes.statement_short: Inner loop: repeat the per-variable update until the residual stops decreasing.

nodes.name: Update each phi_k
nodes.statement: For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;\\
nodes.statement_short: For each $k$, re-estimate $\phi_k(X_k)$ as the conditional expectation of the residual given $X_k$.

nodes.name: End inner loop
nodes.statement: End Inner Iteration Loop;\\
nodes.statement_short: Inner loop terminates.

nodes.name: Update theta
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;\\
nodes.statement_short: Re-estimate $\theta(Y)$ as the normalized conditional expectation of $\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)$ given $Y$.

nodes.name: End outer loop
nodes.statement: End Outer Iteration Loop;\\
nodes.statement_short: Outer loop terminates.

nodes.name: Return solution
nodes.statement: $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;\\
nodes.statement_short: Return the converged $\theta^*,\phi_1^*,\ldots,\phi_p^*$.

nodes.name: Generate channel parameters
nodes.statement: Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$;
nodes.statement_short: Draw random channel parameters $\lambda,\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Compute mutual information
nodes.statement: Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information;
nodes.statement_short: Compute Shannon/Chernoff mutual information for the sampled parameters.

nodes.name: Decompose by ACE
nodes.statement: Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm;
nodes.statement_short: Invoke the ACE algorithm to decompose the information measure.

nodes.name: Repeat
nodes.statement: Repeat above process till the required times.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the whole process for the required number of trials.
